extracted.intended_audience: students and aspiring problem-solvers / math olympiad trainees
extracted.subtask_description: Use the extremal (variational) principle and related heuristics to prove existence/ impossibility results in combinatorics, geometry, number theory and tiling: select a maximal/minimal object and derive contradictions or constructive consequences by small perturbations or counting. The chapter also collects allied methods (well-ordering, coloring, greedy algorithm, infinite descent, counting/partitioning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal principle (variational method)
rubrics_metrics.description: We are trying to prove the existence of an object with certain properties. The extremal principle tells us to pick an object which maximizes or minimizes some function. The resulting object is then shown to have the desired property by showing that a slight perturbation (variation) would further increase or decrease the given function. If there are several optimizing objects, then it is usually immaterial which one we use. In addition, the extremal principle is mostly constructive, giving an algorithm for constructing the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when proving existence or impossibility: select an extremal object (min or max), analyze how any small change would affect the extremal value to derive contradictions or force the desired structure. Examples: E2 (choose vertex with smallest distance to a plane to produce a tetrahedron), E16 (choose maximal circumcircle), E13 (choose dwarf with maximal milk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for invariants under transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a transformation, look for an invariant!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when a process or symmetry is present; invariants can be parity, color classes, sums modulo k, or preserved quantities under moves. The book references the Invariance Principle as a complementary heuristic to the Extremal Principle and uses it in tiling and sharing problems (e.g., milk-sharing problem's rotational invariance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle / use of minimal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonempty subset of positive integers has a smallest element (well-ordering). Every finite nonempty set of nonnegative integers or real numbers has a minimal and maximal element. For real sets sup and inf may be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to pick a least counterexample or smallest element to force structure or to initiate infinite descent arguments (see E9, E17). Explicitly invoked as a foundational tool that underpins extremal/minimal-element reasoning and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-to-one correspondence for counting
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental counting principle is one-to-one correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map difficult-to-count objects bijectively to easy-to-count objects to obtain exact counts. Used in E1 to count parts of plane/space by mapping parts with deepest points to intersection points and mapping unbounded parts to intervals on a horizontal line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greedy algorithm as an extremal construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 'greedy' extremal construction: start with smallest element and iteratively add the smallest admissible element (the minimal choice that keeps required property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to build large structures avoiding forbidden patterns. Example: E15 constructs a sequence with no three-term arithmetic progression by repeatedly adding the smallest integer that doesn't create a progression; leads to representation in ternary without digit 2 and an explicit construction for the contest problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize a global measure to enforce local structure (e.g., minimal total length matching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all configurations, choose one minimizing a natural global quantity (total length, number of inversions, etc.). A local bad configuration (e.g., crossing roads) can be altered to strictly decrease the measure, contradicting minimality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prove existence of noncrossing perfect matching (E4): choose bijection from farms to wells with minimal total road length; any crossing can be uncrossed to shorten total length, hence minimal system has no crossings. This pattern recurs: pick global minimum to forbid local bad patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloring as an invariant / parity argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Color the domain (board, graph, integers modulo k, chessboard or other pattern) so that tiles/objects/operations affect color classes in constrained ways; use counts of colored cells to derive impossibility or bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: coloring rows alternately black/white to show 1×1 tile needed by divisibility (example in chunk), 3-color diagonal coloring for 1×3 tiling contradictions, chessboard coloring of 2×2×2 subcubes to compare black/white counts (E30). Use colorings tailored to the tile shape or symmetry; sometimes multiple colorings/exploiting rotations give stronger constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault-line / edge-breaking counting in tiling problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify potential fault-lines that tiles can 'break'. Show each such fault-line must be broken by at least a certain number of tiles, while each tile can break at most a certain number; use area/count contradiction to rule out tilings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Golomb–Jewett tiling argument (E28) for 6×6 domino tilings: each of 10 potential fault-lines must be broken by at least two tiles; since no tile breaks more than one fault-line, at least 20 tiles are needed, contradicting area. This template applies to many impossibility tiling proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite descent / smallest-counterexample contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a solution exists and choose one with minimal/least value of some measure; show from it one can construct a strictly smaller solution, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical number-theoretic technique illustrated in E9 and E17: pick minimal solution in integers and derive a smaller one via divisibility or algebraic manipulation. Equivalent to well-ordering used to disprove existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count double/overcounting to derive inequalities (face/vertex counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count a combinatorial object from two perspectives (e.g., per-plane contributions and per-tetrahedron contributions) to derive inequalities or exact formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example E2: count tetrahedra by summing how many rest on each plane (numerator) and dividing by 4 because each tetrahedron counted four times (denominator) to get tn ≥ (2n − 3)/4. Use labeling like 'each object contributes r to sum; divide by r' frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitioning into small blocks to get local lower/upper bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the domain into small, simple blocks (2×2 squares, subcubes, L-shaped pieces) and argue a required property in each block (e.g., at least k colored cells or at least one tile crossing), adding up to a global bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in E37 (L–tromino coloring): partition into mn/4 squares of size 2×2 to bound number of colored cells; used also to get lower bounds on number of rooks in Rn via layer arguments (E12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select extremal element to localize structure (e.g., nearest/farthest point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an element extremal relative to some geometry (closest to a line, farthest left then lowest, farthest pair etc.) to force configuration properties or contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated across problems: pick point with minimal distance to a line to prove Sylvester-type results (E10), pick leftmost-lowest point to rule out midpoint property (E5), pick farthest pair for geometry contradictions. Often combined with perpendicular foot or triangle inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of maximality to force coverage (e.g., maximal circumcircle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among finitely many candidate objects (circles through triples of vertices, etc.), choose one with maximal radius/area and deduce that it must cover or satisfy a desired property; otherwise a larger one would exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example E16: pick a maximal circumcircle through three vertices; show it must cover the polygon and pass through three consecutive vertices, via indirect contradiction and maximality argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using averaging / extremal equality to deduce uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the maximal (or minimal) element and compare it to averages of neighbors to deduce equalities; if strict inequalities occur you'd get contradiction, hence all must be equal or in a prescribed pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E13 milk-sharing: pick dwarf with maximal milk x, equate x to average of others' contributions to deduce equality across involved variables and derive explicit distribution. Similar style applies to problems where extremal element equals average of others.
